title: Oklahoma ADA Title II PDF Accessibility: 4 Cities Measured | SignalFeed.dev
description: How Oklahoma cities of 50,000+ stand on PDF accessibility before the April 26, 2027 ADA Title II date: 37% of 198 sampled PDFs untagged, 4% scanned. Aggregate, automated signals.
h1: Oklahoma: Title II PDF backlog in cities of 50,000+
body:
Oklahoma has 8 cities of 50,000 or more residents with an official website listed in Wikidata. Under the ADA Title II web rule (28 CFR part 35, subpart H), a city's date depends on its population in the most recent decennial Census: 50,000 or more means April 26, 2027. Web content, PDFs included, must conform to WCAG 2.1 Level AA, subject to the rule's exceptions. Smaller cities and special districts in Oklahoma have until April 26, 2028 under the current rule.

We measured the PDFs these cities link from their public websites. This page summarizes Oklahoma as a whole. It does not name or rank individual cities.

Oklahoma at a glance

  • 4 of 8 cities measured with a usable sample (20 or more PDFs). The rest blocked automated visitors, host documents on other systems, or had too few PDFs to sample; that is not a clean result.
  • 198 PDFs analyzed. 36.9% had no accessibility tags, lower than the national figure of 40.0%. 3.5% were scanned images with no usable text, and 49.5% did not declare a document language.
  • 0 of 12 sampled PDFs passed the veraPDF PDF/UA-1 checks.
  • The median measured city has roughly 4,300 pages of PDFs failing at least one basic check; across the measured cities that is on the order of 19,000 pages.
  • 48% of the sampled PDFs were modified in 2024 or later. Recent documents are more likely to still be in active use, and documents used to apply for, access or participate in a service are not covered by the rule's exception for preexisting documents.

What this means for a Oklahoma city

An untagged PDF gives a screen reader no headings, no reading order and no table structure. A scanned PDF gives it nothing at all. Both typically fail WCAG 2.1 AA (for example 1.3.1 Info and Relationships, and for scans 1.1.1 Non-text Content), and both are common in agendas, minutes, budgets and forms.

Not every old PDF has to be fixed. The rule exempts archived web content and preexisting conventional electronic documents unless they are currently used to apply for, access or participate in a service. The practical order is usually: fix the export settings so new documents are born accessible, remediate forms and anything people use to get a service, and move true archives to a clearly marked archive section. Our ADA Title II PDF guide walks through it.

For agendas, minutes and notices, our accessible meeting templates for small public bodies ($24, Word + PDF/UA) export tagged PDFs from Word, so new documents start out accessible.

What this is, and what it isn't

These are automated signals, not a conformance evaluation. An automated check can show that a PDF fails; it cannot show that a PDF conforms. Estimates are scaled from samples, and a few very long documents can move a number a lot. The full method is on the national Backlog Index page.
